title: Best Hearing Protection for Fireworks: Adults, Kids, Babies and Dogs
summary: A close-range firework can reach up to 150 to 175 decibels, louder than a jet engine at takeoff and well above the level that causes immediate hearing damage in unprotected ears. The question many parents ask first when it comes to fireworks is simple: how loud are fireworks? The answer is that they are among the loudest sounds most families will experience all year. Whether you're attending a backyard Fourth of July display, a professional fireworks show, a New Year's Eve celebration, or Disney fireworks, the noise levels routinely exceed what hearing experts consider safe without protection. This guide covers: How loud fireworks are in decibels Whether babies and kids need hearing protection The best ear protection for adults, toddlers, and infants Dog ear protection during fireworks NRR ratings and what they actually mean Why AirPods are not hearing protection How to protect your family's hearing during fireworks season AXIL has spent more than a decade designing and manufacturing hearing protection for shooters, NASCAR fans, industrial workers, and concert-goers. Fireworks create a similar challenge: protecting ears from intense impulse noise while remaining comfortable enough to wear through an entire event. How Loud Are Fireworks? The Decibel Reality Professional fireworks typically measure between 150 and 175 decibels at the launch site, while consumer fireworks often peak between 140 and 160 decibels. That places fireworks in the same category as: Gunshots Jet engines Professional racing environments Industrial impulse-noise events Why Are Fireworks So Loud? Fireworks create a rapid chemical explosion inside a confined shell. When that pressure is released, it creates a powerful shockwave that travels through the air. This explosive impulse is why fireworks often sound louder than other sounds with comparable decibel ratings. How Loud Are Fireworks From a Distance? Distance helps, but not as much as many people think. Distance From Launch Approximate dB Level Launch Site 150–175 dB 50 Feet 130–140 dB 200 Feet 110–125 dB 500 Feet 100–110 dB 1,000 Feet 95–105 dB Even at 1,000 feet, prolonged exposure can exceed safe listening thresholds. OSHA and NIOSH both recognize that sustained exposure above safe noise levels can contribute to cumulative and progressive hearing damage. Fireworks vs Other Loud Sounds Sound Approximate dB Conversation 60 dB Rock Concert 110–130 dB Thunder 110–120 dB Fireworks 140–175 dB 12-Gauge Shotgun 145–165 dB Centerfire Rifle 150–175 dB Jet Engine (100 ft) 140+ dB Are Fireworks Louder Than Gunshots? Not necessarily. A centerfire rifle and a professional firework shell can produce similar peak decibel levels. The difference is that a fireworks show can expose you to hundreds of impulse events in a single evening, which increases cumulative exposure. Can Fireworks Cause Permanent Hearing Damage? Yes. Fireworks can cause permanent hearing damage when exposure occurs without adequate hearing protection. Signs of overexposure to hazardous noise include: Ringing ears (tinnitus) Muffled hearing Ear discomfort Difficulty understanding speech after the event Children may not recognize or communicate these symptoms, which is one reason hearing protection is especially important for younger attendees. Are Fireworks Too Loud for Babies, Kids and Newborns? Yes. Fireworks are too loud for babies, newborns, and toddlers without hearing protection. A child's hearing system is still developing, and younger children are particularly vulnerable to impulse noise exposure, particularly for long periods. Age-by-Age Fireworks Hearing Protection Guide Newborn (0–6 mo) Avoid fireworks shows if possible Infant (6–12 mo) NRR 25+ earmuffs Toddler (1–3 yrs) NRR 22–27 earmuffs Child (4–12 yrs) NRR 22–27 earmuffs Teen Adult-rated protection Are Fireworks Too Loud for a 3-Month-Old? Absolutely. Most pediatric hearing experts recommend avoiding public fireworks displays with very young infants whenever possible. If attendance is unavoidable: Use infant-specific earmuffs Stay 500+ feet away Leave immediately if the baby becomes distressed Does My 1-Year-Old Need Ear Protection for Fireworks? Without question. One-year-olds and toddlers should wear properly fitted hearing protection throughout the event. Adult earmuffs generally do not seal properly on a toddler's head and often provide significantly less protection than advertised. What About Pregnancy? Many OB-GYNs recommend maintaining distance from launch areas during late pregnancy. While maternal hearing protection primarily protects the mother, avoiding close-range exposure and maintaining distance from launch sites is generally considered prudent.
